basic_information.name: RAG Security & Adversarial Robustness
basic_information.creator: Cross-disciplinary research and tooling ecosystem. Key contributors: NVIDIA (NeMo Guardrails), Protect AI (LLM Guard), Lakera (Lakera Guard, acquired by Check Point Software Sep 2025), academic teams at Penn State (PoisonedRAG), Tel Aviv University (Machine Against the RAG), Michigan State University (SecureRAG), and standards bodies (OWASP LLM Top 10 2025). No single creator — this entry covers the RAG security landscape as a domain.
basic_information.description: RAG Security & Adversarial Robustness encompasses the full threat model, attack taxonomy, and defense ecosystem for Retrieval-Augmented Generation systems. RAG introduces unique attack surfaces beyond standard LLM security: the external knowledge base can be poisoned (PoisonedRAG achieves 97% attack success with just 5 injected texts among millions), embeddings can be inverted to reconstruct private documents (Zero2Text, ALGEN), retrieval can be jammed with blocker documents (Machine Against the RAG), and indirect prompt injection through retrieved content can hijack LLM behavior without the user's awareness. OWASP's 2025 LLM Top 10 formalized these risks as LLM08: Vector and Embedding Weaknesses, a brand-new category recognizing that RAG's reliance on external data stores creates attack surfaces distinct from prompt injection (LLM01). The defense ecosystem spans open-source toolkits (NeMo Guardrails, LLM Guard), commercial API services (Lakera Guard), academic defense frameworks (GRADA, RAGRank, SecureRAG), and architectural best practices (trust boundaries, context isolation, RBAC on vector stores, encrypted retrieval). For entrepreneurs, RAG security is table stakes for enterprise deployment — 90% of organizations are deploying LLMs but only 5% feel confident in their AI security posture.
basic_information.release_date: Ongoing research domain. Key milestones: OWASP LLM Top 10 v2025 (includes LLM08 Vector & Embedding Weaknesses, published 2025); PoisonedRAG (USENIX Security 2025, arxiv Feb 2024); Machine Against the RAG (USENIX Security 2025, arxiv Jun 2024); GRADA (EMNLP 2025, arxiv May 2025); SecureRAG (NeurIPS 2025); CorruptRAG (arxiv Jan 2026); NeMo Guardrails v0.20.0 (latest as of Feb 2026)
basic_information.license: Varies by tool. NeMo Guardrails: Apache 2.0. LLM Guard: MIT. Lakera Guard: Proprietary (commercial API). Academic papers: open access. OWASP resources: Creative Commons.
basic_information.github_stars: NeMo Guardrails: ~5,200 stars (github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Guardrails). LLM Guard: ~2,500 stars (github.com/protectai/llm-guard). PoisonedRAG: open-source research code (github.com/sleeepeer/PoisonedRAG). Machine Against the RAG: open-source (github.com/avitalsh/jamming_attack). All counts as of February 2026.

technical_architecture.architecture_type: Multi-layered defense architecture. RAG security operates at five layers: (1) Input Layer — prompt injection detection and input sanitization (NeMo input rails, Lakera Guard API); (2) Retrieval Layer — retrieval rails that validate, filter, or reject retrieved chunks before they reach the LLM (NeMo retrieval rails, RBAC on vector stores); (3) Embedding Layer — encrypted search via FHE, attribute-based encryption for access control (SecureRAG), differential privacy on embeddings; (4) Re-ranking Layer — authority-based re-ranking to suppress adversarial documents (RAGRank PageRank, GRADA graph-based reranking); (5) Output Layer — hallucination detection, PII filtering, response grounding verification. Architecturally, security tools are deployed as middleware/interceptors in the RAG pipeline, typically as API calls (Lakera) or in-process libraries (NeMo Guardrails, LLM Guard).
technical_architecture.language: NeMo Guardrails: Python (with Colang DSL for policy definition). LLM Guard: Python. Lakera Guard: Language-agnostic REST API. Academic implementations: primarily Python with PyTorch for attack/defense research.
technical_architecture.embedding_dimensions: Not dimension-specific — RAG security tools operate on any embedding dimension. However, embedding inversion attacks (Zero2Text, ALGEN) work across common dimensions (768, 1024, 1536, 3072). SecureRAG's FHE-based encrypted search adds ~0.05s overhead regardless of embedding dimension.
technical_architecture.indexing_algorithm: Not directly applicable — security tools wrap around existing indexing infrastructure. However, attacks exploit indexing properties: PoisonedRAG optimizes adversarial texts to rank highly under HNSW/IVF similarity search; Machine Against the RAG crafts blocker documents that exploit cosine similarity matching. Defenses like GRADA and RAGRank add graph-based re-ranking layers on top of standard ANN indexes.
technical_architecture.scalability: NeMo Guardrails: supports parallel rails execution (v0.20.0) for reduced latency with multiple concurrent guardrails; integrates with GPU-accelerated NIM microservices for enterprise scale. Lakera Guard: processes 10M+ AI interactions monthly across 200+ enterprise applications; designed for high-throughput API access. LLM Guard: runs locally with no external dependencies, suitable for edge or on-device deployment. Key scaling challenge: security checks add latency to every RAG query — NeMo parallel rails and Lakera's low-latency API (~few ms per call) aim to minimize this overhead.
technical_architecture.deployment_options: NeMo Guardrails: self-hosted (pip install nemoguardrails), Docker/Kubernetes, NVIDIA NIM microservices for enterprise. Lakera Guard: cloud API (SaaS), on-premise or private cloud hosting (Enterprise tier). LLM Guard: self-hosted (pip install llm-guard), Docker, runs entirely locally. SecureRAG: research prototype, self-hosted. For production: most enterprises deploy a combination — Lakera or NeMo for real-time guardrails + LLM Guard for additional local scanning + RBAC at the vector database level.

rag_specific_capabilities.retrieval_method: RAG security tools do not perform retrieval themselves but defend against retrieval exploitation. Key attack vectors on retrieval methods: (1) Dense vector retrieval is vulnerable to adversarial embedding crafting — attackers use gradient-based methods like HotFlip to create 'Vector Magnets' that appear irrelevant to humans but are top-k matches to the retriever; (2) Sparse retrieval (BM25) is vulnerable to keyword stuffing attacks; (3) Hybrid search can be attacked on either or both channels; (4) Knowledge graph retrieval faces KG perturbation attacks that degrade graph structure. NeMo Guardrails retrieval rails intercept and filter retrieved chunks before they reach the LLM. GRADA and RAGRank add defensive re-ranking layers that operate after initial retrieval.
rag_specific_capabilities.chunking_strategy_support: Chunking strategy affects attack surface: larger chunks provide more context for indirect prompt injection; smaller chunks reduce the impact of a single poisoned chunk but require more adversarial injections. Security best practice: document-structure-aware chunking preserves metadata (source, author, timestamp) that enables provenance-based filtering. Retrieval rails in NeMo Guardrails operate at the chunk level — each retrieved chunk can be individually accepted, rejected, or sanitized before aggregation.
rag_specific_capabilities.reranking_support: Defensive re-ranking is a primary mitigation strategy. (1) RAGRank: PageRank-based authority scores over a corpus citation graph, improving accuracy by 10-15 percentage points under poisoning attacks; (2) GRADA (EMNLP 2025): graph-based re-ranking that constructs document-document similarity graphs — adversarial documents appear as outliers with weak inter-document connections, achieving up to 80% reduction in attack success rates across 6 LLMs on Natural Questions; (3) NeMo Guardrails supports cross-encoder and score-fusion reranking as retrieval rails. Standard reranking (cross-encoder, ColBERT) helps but is not specifically designed for adversarial robustness.
rag_specific_capabilities.multimodal_support: Multimodal RAG introduces additional attack surfaces: MM-PoisonRAG (Feb 2025, arxiv 2502.17832) demonstrates local and global knowledge poisoning attacks on multimodal RAG systems targeting vision-language models. Image-based prompt injection can embed malicious instructions in images that are OCR-processed and retrieved. NeMo Guardrails v0.20.0 includes multimodal input/output rails for checking safety of both text and image prompts.
rag_specific_capabilities.graph_rag_support: Knowledge graph RAG (KG-RAG) faces specific attack vectors: adversarial entity injection, relationship poisoning, and structural perturbation of the knowledge graph. Research demonstrates that minimal KG perturbations (adding/modifying a few edges) can significantly degrade KG-RAG performance. GRADA's graph-based defense approach is particularly relevant to GraphRAG as it already operates on graph structures. No dedicated GraphRAG security framework exists yet — this is an active research area.
rag_specific_capabilities.citation_grounding: Citation and grounding serve as both evaluation metrics and defense mechanisms. RAGAS faithfulness metric measures whether generated responses are grounded in retrieved context (0-1 score). NeMo Guardrails provides fact-checking rails that verify response grounding. Lakera Guard includes output validation that checks response consistency with retrieved sources. RAGRank uses citation graphs for authority scoring — documents with more citations from trusted sources receive higher authority, making them harder for adversarial injections to outrank.
rag_specific_capabilities.context_window_optimization: Security considerations for context window: (1) Adversarial documents are designed to consume context window space, displacing legitimate information (Machine Against the RAG 'blocker' documents); (2) Context compression must preserve security-relevant metadata; (3) Summarization of retrieved chunks before injection can strip adversarial prompt injection payloads but may also remove legitimate instructions. NeMo retrieval rails filter out suspicious chunks before they consume context window capacity, effectively defending the context window as a resource.

performance_and_benchmarks.latency: Security adds overhead to RAG queries. NeMo Guardrails: parallel rail execution reduces latency; typical 50-200ms overhead for input + retrieval + output rails combined (varies with number and complexity of rails). Lakera Guard: low-latency API, typically <50ms per API call for prompt injection detection. LLM Guard: 20-100ms per scanner depending on model complexity. SecureRAG: +0.05s overhead for FHE encrypted search. The total security overhead for a well-configured pipeline is typically 100-300ms on top of base RAG latency, which is acceptable for most applications but may be significant for real-time chat at scale.
performance_and_benchmarks.throughput: Lakera Guard: 10M+ AI interactions monthly across production deployments. NeMo Guardrails: enterprise-grade throughput with GPU-accelerated NIM microservices. LLM Guard: throughput limited by local compute; suitable for moderate traffic. For attack benchmarks: PoisonedRAG can poison a knowledge base of millions of documents by injecting just 5 texts per target question (processing takes seconds for text generation). GRADA defense evaluation: tested on Natural Questions with 6 LLMs, processing thousands of attack/defense evaluation pairs.
performance_and_benchmarks.accuracy_metrics: Attack success rates (higher = more vulnerable): PoisonedRAG achieves 97% (NQ), 99% (HotpotQA), 91% (MS-MARCO) attack success with 5 injected texts. CorruptRAG achieves higher success rates than PoisonedRAG with only 1 injected text per query. Machine Against the RAG: single blocker document can jam specific queries. Defense effectiveness: GRADA reduces attack success rates by up to 80% while maintaining retrieval accuracy. RAGRank improves accuracy by 10-15 percentage points under poisoning. Lakera Guard: 99.7% detection rate for malicious prompts. NeMo Guardrails: 89% accuracy on prompt injection detection tests (16/18 adversarial questions blocked).
performance_and_benchmarks.benchmark_results: No unified benchmark exists for RAG security. Key evaluation datasets used across papers: Natural Questions (NQ), HotpotQA, MS-MARCO for poisoning attacks; OWASP LLM benchmark prompts for injection detection. Emerging benchmarks: (1) Benchmarking Poisoning Attacks against RAG (arxiv 2505.18543, May 2025) — first systematic comparison of RAG poisoning methods; (2) FaithBench for hallucination detection (EMNLP 2025) — o3-mini-high judge achieves 84% balanced accuracy, 82.1% F1-macro; (3) OWASP provides structured red-teaming frameworks. The Lakera prompt injection benchmark and Giskard's LLM vulnerability scanner provide practical testing frameworks. [uncertain]

integration_and_ecosystem.framework_compatibility: NeMo Guardrails: native integration with LangChain, LangGraph, LlamaIndex; supports multi-agent deployments. LLM Guard: standalone library, integrates with any Python RAG pipeline; works with LangChain and LlamaIndex via wrapper functions. Lakera Guard: REST API compatible with any framework; official integrations with LangChain, LlamaIndex, and Haystack. OWASP provides framework-agnostic security checklists applicable to any RAG implementation. Giskard integrates with LangChain, LlamaIndex, and Haystack for automated vulnerability scanning.
integration_and_ecosystem.model_compatibility: NeMo Guardrails: compatible with OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Mistral, open-source models via vLLM/Ollama; supports reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1) and the NemoGuard JailbreakDetect NIM. Lakera Guard: model-agnostic API that works with any LLM provider. LLM Guard: supports OpenAI, Anthropic, local models; uses its own detection models for some scanners. The security tools are generally model-agnostic — they intercept inputs/outputs regardless of the underlying LLM.
integration_and_ecosystem.mcp_integration_status: No dedicated MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers found for RAG security tools as of February 2026. However, NeMo Guardrails' architecture is compatible with MCP-style integration patterns, and securing MCP layers is an active concern — the IEEE S&P 2026 paper 'When AI Meets the Web' addresses prompt injection risks in third-party AI chatbot plugins, which is directly relevant to MCP security. [uncertain]
integration_and_ecosystem.data_source_connectors: RAG security tools operate on the RAG pipeline's data flow rather than connecting to data sources directly. NeMo Guardrails: intercepts any data flowing through the RAG pipeline. Lakera Guard: scans any text input via API, applicable to data from S3, GCS, Confluence, Notion, Slack, web crawl, etc. SecureRAG: designed for encrypted retrieval from vector databases. The security layer is data-source-agnostic — it operates on the text content regardless of origin.
integration_and_ecosystem.observability_integration: NeMo Guardrails: migrated to OpenTelemetry (v0.20.0) for standardized observability; compatible with any OTEL-compliant monitoring stack. Lakera Guard: provides compliance reporting for SOC 2, GDPR, HIPAA; built-in logging and alerting dashboard. Langfuse: provides an LLM Security & Guardrails integration page listing compatible tools (NeMo, Lakera, LLM Guard, Guardrails AI). LLM Guard: logs all scanner results for audit trails. For production: teams typically combine RAGAS evaluation metrics + Langfuse/LangSmith tracing + Lakera/NeMo guardrails logging for comprehensive security observability.

pricing_and_cost.pricing_model: Mixed ecosystem: Open-source tools: NeMo Guardrails (free, Apache 2.0), LLM Guard (free, MIT) — zero licensing cost, self-hosted compute only. Commercial API: Lakera Guard — Developer (free, 10K API calls/month), Pro (from $99/month, higher volume + advanced detection), Enterprise (custom pricing, unlimited calls, on-premise option, custom models, SLA). Enterprise: NVIDIA NIM microservices for NeMo Guardrails (contact NVIDIA for enterprise pricing). Cloud provider security: Azure AI Content Safety, AWS Bedrock Guardrails — included in cloud provider pricing tiers.
pricing_and_cost.free_tier: NeMo Guardrails: entirely free and open-source (Apache 2.0), no usage limits. LLM Guard: entirely free and open-source (MIT), no usage limits. Lakera Guard Developer: free tier with 10,000 API calls/month, access to core detection models. Azure AI Content Safety: free tier available within Azure credits. Giskard: open-source vulnerability scanner, free.
pricing_and_cost.cost_at_scale: Self-hosted open-source (NeMo + LLM Guard): compute costs only — approximately $50-500/month on cloud GPU instances for medium-traffic RAG applications. Lakera Guard Pro: starting at $99/month for moderate production traffic. Lakera Guard Enterprise: custom pricing for 10M+ interactions/month (likely $1,000-10,000+/month range based on enterprise AI security market rates). Full security stack for a startup (NeMo Guardrails self-hosted + Lakera Developer + RAGAS evaluation): $0-200/month. Enterprise-grade (Lakera Enterprise + NeMo NIM + observability): $2,000-20,000/month depending on traffic volume. [uncertain]
pricing_and_cost.total_cost_of_ownership: For a startup building a secure RAG application: (1) Security tooling: $0-200/month (open-source stack) to $1,000-10,000/month (enterprise commercial); (2) Engineering time: 2-6 weeks to implement comprehensive security layer (significant hidden cost); (3) Ongoing maintenance: security rules need updating as attack techniques evolve; (4) Compliance overhead: SOC 2, GDPR documentation if using Lakera or similar; (5) LLM costs for security checks: some guardrails use LLM calls for classification, adding $50-500/month in API costs. Critical insight: the cost of NOT implementing RAG security (data breach, hallucination liability, regulatory fines under EU AI Act) far exceeds the tooling cost. The EU AI Act's staged obligations through 2026-2027 make security investment non-optional for European deployments.

adoption_and_market.market_position: RAG security is an emerging but rapidly formalizing discipline. The field transitioned from academic curiosity (2023-2024) to enterprise imperative (2025-2026) driven by: OWASP LLM Top 10 2025 formalizing vector/embedding weaknesses as LLM08, EU AI Act obligations taking effect, and high-profile attack demonstrations (PoisonedRAG, Machine Against the RAG at USENIX Security 2025). Market leaders: Lakera Guard (acquired by Check Point Software Sep 2025 for undisclosed amount — strongest signal of market maturity), NVIDIA NeMo Guardrails (largest open-source footprint with 5.2K stars), LLM Guard by Protect AI (2.5K stars, 2.5M+ downloads). The broader AI security market was valued at $22.4B in 2023 with 21.9% CAGR. RAG-specific security is a sub-segment growing faster than the overall market.

adoption_and_market.competitive_landscape: Layered competitive landscape: (1) Open-source frameworks: NeMo Guardrails (NVIDIA, most feature-complete), LLM Guard (Protect AI, widest adoption), Rebuff (multi-layer prompt injection defense), Giskard (vulnerability scanning); (2) Commercial API: Lakera Guard (acquired by Check Point, market leader), PromptArmor, Calypso AI; (3) Cloud provider built-in: Azure AI Content Safety, AWS Bedrock Guardrails, Google Vertex AI safety filters; (4) Academic defenses: GRADA (graph reranking, EMNLP 2025), RAGRank (PageRank authority, Oct 2025), SecureRAG (FHE encrypted retrieval, NeurIPS 2025), ReliabilityRAG (provably robust defense). Key differentiators: NeMo Guardrails excels at customizable policy definition via Colang DSL; Lakera leads in enterprise deployment and detection accuracy (99.7%); LLM Guard wins on ease of integration and local-first privacy; academic defenses lead in novel defense mechanisms but lack production readiness.

entrepreneurial_relevance.startup_applicability: Critical for any startup deploying RAG in production, especially those handling sensitive data (healthcare, legal, finance) or targeting enterprise customers. Team size: a single security-aware engineer can implement NeMo Guardrails + LLM Guard in 1-2 weeks. Budget: $0 to start with open-source tools; $99-500/month for Lakera Pro when scaling to production. Use case fit: mandatory for enterprise sales (customers will ask about security posture), regulated industries, applications where incorrect answers carry liability (medical, legal, financial RAG). Not critical for: internal-only prototypes, non-sensitive information retrieval, early MVPs before product-market fit. The 90% of organizations deploying LLMs with only 5% feeling confident in AI security represents a massive opportunity — startups that can demonstrate robust RAG security have a competitive advantage in enterprise sales.
entrepreneurial_relevance.build_vs_buy_guidance: Recommended approach by stage: (1) MVP/POC: use open-source stack only — NeMo Guardrails for input/retrieval/output rails + LLM Guard for PII detection. Cost: $0 + compute. Time: 1-2 weeks. (2) Early production: add Lakera Guard Developer tier (free, 10K calls/month) for real-time prompt injection detection on top of open-source stack. (3) Scale/Enterprise: upgrade to Lakera Pro or Enterprise for SLA, compliance reporting, on-premise option. Add RBAC at the vector database level (Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant all support namespace-level access control). (4) Regulated industries: consider SecureRAG-style FHE encryption for maximum privacy (research prototype, not production-ready yet). Never build your own prompt injection detector from scratch — the attack landscape evolves too fast. Do customize NeMo Guardrails policies (Colang DSL) for your specific domain.
entrepreneurial_relevance.time_to_production: Basic guardrails (NeMo input/output rails): 2-3 days. Retrieval rails + chunk filtering: 1 week. Full security stack (NeMo + LLM Guard + Lakera + RBAC): 2-4 weeks. Compliance documentation (SOC 2, GDPR): 1-3 months. Ongoing: security rules require regular updates as new attack vectors emerge (budget 1-2 days per month for security maintenance). The fastest path to 'secure enough for enterprise demo' is 1 week using NeMo Guardrails with pre-built rail configurations.
key_lessons: RAG security is not optional for enterprise deployment — OWASP LLM Top 10 2025 formalized vector/embedding weaknesses (LLM08) as a top-tier risk, and the EU AI Act's staged obligations through 2026-2027 make security compliance mandatory. Start implementing security from day one, not as an afterthought.

Layer your defenses: no single tool stops all attacks. Use NeMo Guardrails for policy-based input/retrieval/output control, LLM Guard for PII/toxicity scanning, and RBAC at the vector database level. Treat RAG security like email anti-phishing: expect evasion, layer controls across every stage of the pipeline.

Knowledge base poisoning is frighteningly effective (PoisonedRAG: 97% success with 5 injected texts, CorruptRAG: high success with just 1 text) — implement provenance tracking and authority-based re-ranking (GRADA, RAGRank) for any knowledge base that accepts external or user-contributed content.

Embedding inversion is a real privacy risk — attackers can reconstruct original text from vector embeddings (Zero2Text, ALGEN). If your vector database contains sensitive data (PII, trade secrets, medical records), consider encrypted vector search (SecureRAG-style FHE) or at minimum, never expose raw embedding APIs publicly.

The cost of RAG security tooling ($0-500/month for startups using open-source) is negligible compared to the cost of a security incident (regulatory fines, customer trust loss, liability). Lakera's acquisition by Check Point ($18B+ company) signals that RAG security is becoming a must-have enterprise capability, not a nice-to-have.
entrepreneurial_relevance.no_code_interface: NeMo Guardrails: no visual UI, but Colang DSL is designed to be readable by non-developers (Python-like policy definitions). Lakera Guard: provides a web dashboard for monitoring and configuration, closest to no-code for security policies. LLM Guard: Python library, no visual interface. Giskard: provides a web UI for vulnerability scanning results. No fully no-code RAG security builder exists as of Feb 2026 — security configuration still requires engineering involvement.
entrepreneurial_relevance.session_mapping: Session 1 (Fundamentals — introduce RAG security as part of the AI landscape, OWASP Top 10 overview), Session 3 (Framing AI projects — security as a non-negotiable part of RAG project planning, Build vs Buy for security tooling), Session 5 (Ethics & governance — EU AI Act implications for RAG security, knowledge base poisoning as an ethical concern, responsible AI deployment)

confidence.data_quality: High — information sourced from peer-reviewed publications at top venues (USENIX Security 2025, NeurIPS 2025, EMNLP 2025, IEEE S&P 2026), OWASP official documentation (genai.owasp.org), official tool documentation (NeMo Guardrails docs, Lakera blog, Protect AI), GitHub repositories with verified star counts, and enterprise security reports (Cloud Security Alliance, CrowdStrike). Attack success rates are from controlled experiments in published papers.
confidence.cross_reference: PoisonedRAG results verified across USENIX proceedings, arxiv (2402.07867), and GitHub repository. OWASP LLM08 confirmed across multiple independent analyses (IronCore Labs, Cobalt, Indusface, Promptfoo). NeMo Guardrails version and features confirmed via GitHub releases page and NVIDIA official documentation. Lakera acquisition by Check Point confirmed via Crunchbase and TechCrunch. confidence.caveats: RAG security is evolving extremely rapidly — new attack vectors and defenses emerge monthly. Academic defenses (GRADA, RAGRank, SecureRAG) are research prototypes not yet production-hardened. Attack success rates (PoisonedRAG 97%, CorruptRAG) are measured in controlled experimental settings and may differ in real-world deployments with diverse knowledge bases. NeMo Guardrails' 89% prompt injection detection rate was measured on a small test set (18 questions). Lakera's 99.7% detection rate is self-reported. SecureRAG's FHE approach adds overhead and is not yet practical for high-throughput production systems. The competitive landscape changes frequently — Lakera's acquisition by Check Point (Sep 2025) may change its product direction. Enterprise pricing for Lakera Guard and NeMo NIM microservices is not publicly disclosed.
confidence.security_posture: This entry IS about the security posture of RAG systems. Key attack surfaces: (1) Knowledge base poisoning — PoisonedRAG (97% success), CorruptRAG (single-text attack), data injection through user-contributed content; (2) Embedding inversion — Zero2Text, ALGEN can reconstruct source text from embeddings, threatening data privacy; (3) Indirect prompt injection — malicious instructions embedded in retrieved documents hijack LLM behavior, up to 80% success rate in real-world tests; (4) Retrieval jamming — Machine Against the RAG uses blocker documents to deny service on specific queries; (5) Unauthorized data access — semantic queries can retrieve confidential embeddings without direct access controls. Built-in mitigations: NeMo Guardrails (input/retrieval/output rails, Colang policies), Lakera Guard (99.7% malicious prompt detection, SOC 2/GDPR/HIPAA compliance), LLM Guard (PII detection, toxicity scanning), GRADA (80% attack reduction via graph reranking), RAGRank (10-15% accuracy improvement via authority scoring), SecureRAG (FHE encrypted retrieval with 0.05s overhead). Compliance: OWASP LLM08:2025 provides the threat model; EU AI Act imposes legal obligations for high-risk AI systems deploying RAG.
